new_statements.quote: Impressionistically, there is a prominence on the penultimate syllable in ChN. [...] This perceived prominence, however, appears to meet Hyman's criteria: all words have at least one primary prominence (the penult), and each word has only one such prominence. The data in (18) show a set of morphologically related words, where stress is regularly on the penultimate syllable as additional morphological material occurs on the right edge. Stress position is thus fixed. [...] The important point here is that stress assignment is fixed and is thus assumed to be postlexical [...] Monosyllabic words appear to have stress as well. [...] Proclitics appear to fall outside of the prosodic word and do not carry primary stress.
new_statements.citation: Aguilar, Andrés Ehecatl. 2020. Phonology and Phonetics of Laryngeal Sounds in Chicontepec Nahuatl. PhD dissertation, University of California San Diego (committee: G. Caballero, M. Garellek, co-chairs). https://escholarship.org/uc/item/27r2x19w
new_statements.locator: Chapter 3, section 3.2.3 'Stress', pp. 42-46 (quoted sentences pp. 43-46); also p. 41 ('stress assignment will always land on the penultimate syllable.. regardless of vowel length')
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the text we hold layer (extracted text of the 46 MB eScholarship PDF, also held). Section 3.2.3 'Stress' begins at the text layer (printed p. 42). Every quoted sentence is present verbatim at the stated locator: 'Impressionistically, there is a prominence on the penultimate syllable in ChN.' (l. 2721, p. 43); 'This perceived prominence, however, appears to meet Hyman's criteria: all words have at least one primary prominence (the penult), and each word has only one such prominence. The data in (18) [fn 14] show a set of morphologically related words, where stress is regularly on the penultimate syllable as additional morphological material occurs on the right edge. Stress position is…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (prosodic) word, irrespective of vowel length and of how many suffixes are added (kóchi, koch-míki, kochmi-kíya; místoh, mis-tónmeh, pilmiston-tsítsi); monosyllables bear stress; proclitics (e.g. negative ax=, yon=) are outside the prosodic word and are not counted, so a proclitic+monosyllable has final stress (ax=tlén). Acoustic correlate: f0 and intensity peak on the penult, drop on the final.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Aguilar only remarks that proclitics 'seem to have some sort of prominence, perhaps secondary stress'; Velázquez Patiño 2016 mentions trochaic binary rhythm generating secondary stress but gives no rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllables (stressed on their only syllable); host after a proclitic keeps its own stress (ax=ˈtlen); 'rare words with final stress' — stressed word-final nasals occur in monosyllables and Spanish loanwords (2020 fn. 27; 2026 p. 166).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word including suffixes but excluding proclitics; evidence from words in isolation (elicitation) with pitch/intensity tracks; author flags the stress marks as impressionistic, supported by one acoustic illustration (Fig. 7).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes Chicontepec Nahuatl (municipality of Chicontepec, Veracruz), which the author identifies explicitly as 'a variety of Eastern Huasteca Nahuatl' (nhe, east2538). Beller & Beller 1979 (not opened) describes mainly Huautla, Hidalgo, also nhe per Glottolog's note, with remarks on Western Huasteca (nhw). The SIL México web statement is family-level (Nahuatl in general) and only corroborative.

sources.note: Dedicated section 3.2.3 'Stress' (pp. 42-46): impressionistic prominence on the penultimate syllable; stress stays penultimate as suffixes are added ('Stress position is thus fixed'); pitch/intensity peak on the penult (Fig. 7); monosyllables stressed; proclitics outside the prosodic word and do not attract stress; 'rare words with final stress' (loanwords, monosyllables) noted in ch. on nasals.
